pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Anthracnose leaf blight is caused by the fungal pathogen Colletotrichum graminicola

type_of_disease.quote: Anthracnose leaf blight is caused by the fungal pathogen Colletotrichum graminicola

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms begin on lower corn leaves early in the growing season and then develop on the upper leaves late in the season. The causal pathogen of anthracnose leaf blight also produces a stalk rot and top dieback.

summary.value: Oval or spindle-shaped leaf lesions with tan or brown centers and dark brown or purple margins, up to 1 inch long and ½ inch wide. Lesions can enlarge and join to blight entire leaves. As disease develops, black spiny fruiting structures appear on dead leaf tissue.
summary.quote: Leaf lesions are oval or spindle shaped, tan or brown with dark brown or purple margins, up to 1 inch long and ½ inch wide. As the disease develops, the fungus produces black, spiny fruiting structures on the dead leaf tissue.

diagnostic_features.value: Black, spiny fruiting structures visible with a 30X hand lens on dead tissue; oval or spindle-shaped lesions with distinctive dark brown or purple margins.
diagnostic_features.quote: the fungus produces black, spiny fruiting structures on the dead leaf tissue. These are visible with a 30X hand lens. Leaf lesions are oval or spindle shaped, tan or brown with dark brown or purple margins

look_alikes.quote: Immature lesions are not diagnostic and can easily be confused with Gray Leaf Spot or Eye spot.

conflicts.canonical_value: Oval or spindle-shaped leaf lesions with tan or brown centers and dark brown or purple margins, up to 1 inch long and ½ inch wide.
conflicts.alternative_value: Water-soaked, oval lesions with tan centers and reddish-brown borders that can enlarge up to 5-6 inches long and may join and blight the entire leaf.
conflicts.note: UMN Extension describes lesions as water-soaked with reddish-brown borders up to 5-6 inches; CPN describes oval/spindle-shaped with dark brown or purple margins up to 1 inch. Difference may reflect early vs. late stage.

conflicts.alternative_value: Colletotrichum graminicola (Ces.) G. W. Wils. (Teleomorph: Glomerella graminicola Politis)
conflicts.note: CropWatch UNL provides full author citation and teleomorph name Glomerella graminicola Politis.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Anthracnose, caused by the fungus Colletotrichum graminicola

type_of_disease.quote: The fungal pathogen Colletotrichum graminicola is the causal agent of anthracnose in corn.

affected_parts.quote: Anthracnose can cause leaf blight, top dieback, and stalk rot... Lesions are often found on the bottom leaves first... The fungus can infect roots from the soil... the pith and the vascular system decay

summary.value: Anthracnose manifests in three phases: leaf blight with tan to brown oval lesions and black hair-like fungal structures (setae), top dieback causing stalk death above the ear, and stalk rot with shiny black discoloration and internal decay of pith and vascular tissue. In the leaf blight phase, small round to irregular water-soaked spots first appear on lower leaves, turning yellow then brown with reddish-brown borders.
summary.quote: Anthracnose can cause leaf blight, top dieback, and stalk rot... Lesions are often tan to brown with yellow to reddish-brown borders... Small, black, hair-like fungal structures called setae often occur in necrotic tissues... a condition that causes stalk death above the ear... a shiny, black discoloration develops in blotches or streaks on the stalk surface

diagnostic_features.value: Black setae (hair-like fungal structures) visible with a hand lens from necrotic leaf lesions; shiny black discoloration in blotches or streaks on lower stalk internodes that cannot be scraped off with a fingernail; shredded pith internally in stalk rot phase.
diagnostic_features.quote: Small, black, hair-like fungal structures called setae often occur in necrotic tissues and can be seen with the help of a hand lens... If removing the sheaths reveals that the stalk has black spots or streaks that can not be removed with a fingernail, the plant is likely infected... a shiny, black discoloration develops in blotches or streaks on the stalk surface, particularly on lower internodes... Internal stalk tissue also may become discolored and soft, starting at the nodes

look_alikes.quote: Small, round to irregular, water-soaked spots first appear on lower leaves. Spots later turn yellow and then brown with reddish-brown borders.

conflicts.note: Bayer source contains a typographical misspelling 'Colletotirchum'; correct spelling is Colletotrichum as confirmed by University of Kentucky source.
University of Kentucky source mentions only foliar and stem phases; Bayer source additionally lists root infection and vascular decay. CPN source lists root and stem only for the stalk rot phase.

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Bacterial brown spot of bean

summary.quote: The primary symptoms on leaves are elongated tan lesions with irregular margins extending parallel to the veins. Large sections of leaf area can be affected. In plants with stalk infection, orange vascular bundles may be seen in the stalk.

diagnostic_features.value: Shiny patches of dried bacterial ooze resembling dry varnish on leaf lesions; dark green to black discontinuous water-soaked spots ('freckles') within lesion margins that appear as transparent spots when observed against light; elongated tan lesions extending parallel to leaf veins; orange vascular bundles visible in infected stalks.
diagnostic_features.quote: A closer look at the lesions reveal dark green to black, discontinuous, water soaked spots (freckles) in the margin of the lesion. When these "freckles" are observed against the light, transparent spots can be seen. These lesions can coalesce forming larger lesions.

The stalk rots completely and the top collapses, causing lodging.

Disease then develops in the stalk and rapidly spreads up the stalk and into the leaves. As the decay progresses, a foul odor can be detected and the top of the plant can be very easily removed from the rest of the plant. The stalk rots completely and the top collapses.

diagnostic_features.quote: Splitting the stalk reveals internal discoloration and soft slimy rot mostly initiating at the nodes. As the decay progresses, a foul odor can be detected

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: It is caused primarily by the fungus Aspergillus flavus, but a few other Aspergillus species may be involved.

diagnostic_features.quote: The fungal spores appear powdery and may disperse like dust when you pull back the husk. These signs are most commonly observed at the tip of the ear, but can be scattered throughout the ear and all the way to the base of the ear.

summary.quote: Fusarium ear rot results in white to salmon-pink discoloration of individual kernels or groups of kernels scattered over the ear. A white to pinkish weft of mycelia covers the kernels, especially on the tip of the ear.

summary.value: Leaves display irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles alternating with parallel veins, ranging from narrow pale-yellow streaks to complete chlorosis, with severely infected leaves turning yellow or yellow-white. Tips of new leaves may become abnormally twisted.
summary.quote: there are many irregular yellow and green inlays, stripes, or mottles alternate with parallel veins on symptomatic leaves, more clearly visible against the sunlight. Some are mostly normal green with only a few narrow pale-yellow streaks, some show very obvious whole leaf chlorosis, and the seriously infected leaves turn yellow or yellow white, leaving only a few green islets or a small amount of red punctate necrosis, or the tips of new leaves are abnormally twisted

diagnostic_features.value: Symptoms are especially visible in the middle and lower sections of new leaves and are more clearly visible when examined against sunlight. Symptoms may be cryptic or indistinct at high temperature but recur when temperature drops.
diagnostic_features.quote: The symptoms of mosaic disease caused by SCMV, SrMV and SCSMV are similar, especially in the middle and lower sections of new leaves... more clearly visible against the sunlight... Some varieties show cryptic or indistinct phenomena at a high temperature, but the symptoms recur as the temperature drops

pathogen_scientific_name.quote: Tar spot of corn, caused by the fungal pathogen Phyllachora maydis, is an important foliar disease in the United States.

type_of_disease.quote: caused by the fungal pathogen Phyllachora maydis

affected_parts.quote: Symptoms of tar spot include yellow to tan flecks on corn leaves, husks, or stalks.

summary.value: Yellow to tan flecks on corn leaves, husks, or stalks with black, glossy, raised fungal fruiting bodies (stromata). Necrotic halos develop around stromata creating fisheye lesions; in severe cases these coalesce to cause leaf blight and premature senescence.
summary.quote: Symptoms of tar spot include yellow to tan flecks on corn leaves, husks, or stalks. The black, glossy, raised fungal fruiting bodies (stromata) of P. maydis are embedded in host tissue, typically circular or oval in shape, and can appear on both upper and lower leaf surfaces... a necrotic halo may develop later around the stromata, giving the appearance of a fisheye lesion... In severe cases, these necrotic halos coalesce, causing leaf blight that leads to premature senescence

diagnostic_features.value: Black, glossy, raised fungal fruiting bodies (stromata) typically circular or oval in shape, embedded in host tissue, appearing on both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Stromata become visible two to three weeks after infection and are surrounded by a distinctive necrotic halo creating a fisheye lesion appearance.
diagnostic_features.quote: The black, glossy, raised fungal fruiting bodies (stromata) of P. maydis are embedded in host tissue, typically circular or oval in shape, and can appear on both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Stromata become visible two to three weeks after infection, and a necrotic halo may develop later around the stromata, giving the appearance of a fisheye lesion.
